summary: Gives recommendations for switches that snoop on IGMP and MLD messages to work out which ports need which multicast traffic. It builds on best current practice for IGMPv2, with extra considerations for IGMPv3 and MLDv2 snooping and for link-layer topology changes. This is informational guidance.

plainLanguage.summary: A switch can observe multicast membership messages to learn which ports have listeners for a group. This memo recommends how to use that information without disrupting routers, hosts, or other multicast traffic.

subtitle: Recommendations for switches that learn multicast membership by observing IGMP and MLD messages.

tldr.problem: Ordinary switching can flood multicast packets onto segments where no device wants them, wasting bandwidth.
tldr.mechanism: An IGMP or MLD snooping switch observes membership and query messages, tracks listener and router ports, and applies forwarding rules for multicast data.
tldr.outcome: The memo gives implementation recommendations for IGMP versions and MLD, including handling topology changes and unknown groups. It is Informational guidance.

today: RFC 4541 is Informational. The work-unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: Why Switches Snoop Multicast
sections.content:
Traditional bridging forwards a multicast packet to every eligible port. That approach reaches all potential listeners, but it also sends traffic to network segments where no node has joined the group. The memo describes snooping switches that inspect Internet Group Management Protocol (IGMP) messages for IPv4 multicast and Multicast Listener Discovery (MLD) messages for IPv6 multicast.

The recommendations focus on IGMPv2 practice, with additional considerations for IGMPv3 and MLDv2. The memo stresses that IGMP snooping should affect IPv4 multicast only and should not change the ordinary forwarding of non-IPv4 multicast packets.
sections.plainLanguage: A switch can avoid sending every multicast packet everywhere by learning where listeners are. IGMP is used for IPv4 groups, while IPv6 uses MLD.

sections.title: Forwarding Membership and Query Messages
sections.content:
A snooping switch should forward IGMP Membership Reports to ports where multicast routers are attached, not simply to other host ports. This matters because IGMPv1 and IGMPv2 hosts can suppress their own reports after hearing another host's report. The switch must maintain a router-port list, learned from router discovery, queries, or administrative configuration.

The switch must not reject membership reports solely because their source address is 0.0.0.0. It should flood unrecognized IGMP messages rather than guess how to interpret them, and it should account for spanning-tree changes that may require refreshed queries. It must not use packets with checksum or integrity errors to update forwarding state, and should age membership entries with a configurable timeout rather than rely only on Leave messages.
sections.plainLanguage: Membership reports need to reach multicast routers so the network can keep accurate group information. A switch must handle unknown messages and topology changes carefully.

sections.title: Forwarding Multicast Data
sections.content:
For multicast destinations outside the IPv4 224.0.0.X range, packets should follow group membership tables and also reach router ports. Packets in the 224.0.0.X range that are not IGMP should be forwarded on all ports, because hosts and routers may use these link-local groups without sending joins.

An unregistered IPv4 multicast packet has a destination group not found in earlier membership reports. The switch must send such packets to router ports; it may also flood them more widely. The memo recommends IP-address-based forwarding when available, because one Ethernet multicast address can correspond to multiple IPv4 multicast addresses. Non-IPv4 multicast continues to use normal bridging behavior.
sections.plainLanguage: Known multicast groups can be sent to listener ports and router ports. Link-local groups and some unknown traffic need broader forwarding so that existing uses are not cut off.

sections.title: IGMP Versions and IPv6 MLD
sections.content:
A switch that does not understand IGMPv3 membership reports may either flood traffic unnecessarily or prune traffic that listeners need. The memo recommends that switches recognize IGMPv3 joins, even if they handle them with the simpler group-level behavior used for IGMPv2. Where an IGMPv3 router is connected through an IGMPv2-only snooping switch that cannot process v3 reports, the memo recommends configuring the router for IGMPv2 or disabling snooping.

MLD snooping follows similar principles for IPv6, but MLD uses ICMPv6 message types. A switch must distinguish MLD from other ICMPv6 traffic and should prefer IP-address-based forwarding because IPv6 multicast addresses can map ambiguously to link-layer addresses. The memo gives special forwarding guidance for all-hosts link-scope traffic and unspecified source addresses.
sections.plainLanguage: Different IGMP versions can expose gaps in a switch's understanding of group membership. MLD has a similar role for IPv6, but the switch must avoid treating every ICMPv6 message as multicast control traffic.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Forged IGMP messages can reduce or remove the bandwidth benefits of snooping. For example, a forged query with a lower source address can affect where reports are sent, and a forged membership report can make the switch believe a listener exists on a segment.

The memo's stated worst-case effect of these attacks is loss of the performance improvement that snooping provides; it says this is no worse than behavior on a network without multicast snooping. It also recommends forwarding membership reports to multicast routers, not only to the current querier.
sections.plainLanguage: False membership messages can make the switch send traffic to the wrong places. The main risk described here is wasted bandwidth and reduced snooping benefit.
